newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-court weighs Dutch use of anonymous witnesses.
newsitem.headline: Euro-court weighs Dutch use of anonymous witnesses.

text.p: Four Dutch nationals asked the European Court of Human Rights on Thursday to rule that the Dutch justice system's use of anonymous witnesses violated their rights.

Should the court rule against it in a decision expected at a later date, the Netherlands would have to alter its use of anonymous testimony to comply with the 1950 European Convention on Human Rights.

The four were each sentenced to 10 years in jail in 1989 after being convicted of robbery and manslaughter on the basis of statements by police officers whose identities were known only to the judge in the case.
The 11 anonymous officers argued they needed to conceal their identities so they could continue to carry out their duties without fear of reprisal.

The judge noted that attorneys for the accused had been able to question the anonymous witnesses through an intercom system and concluded that the officers had sufficient reason to protect their anonymity.

The trial judge's ruling was upheld on appeal, and the European Commission of Human Rights, which screens cases for the European rights court, concluded by a vote of 20 to eight that there had been no violation of the 1950 rights convention.
The court and the commission are both part of the 40-nation Council of Europe, set up after World War Two to promote democracy and human rights across Europe.
